facts.statement: Artist, reporter and student of birchbark canoes, 1868–1950.
Reported the Klondike gold rush; The Klondike Stampede published 1900.
Worked in New Brunswick and documented indigenous canoe-building traditions.

interpretation.note: Interpretation of the documented life and works; no claim of personal acquaintance from shared themes.

appraisal.note: AETERNUS editorial judgement; not presented as a historical quotation.

en.tagline: A gold rush observed with the eye of a draughtsman.
en.intro: Adney brought drawing, reporting and close description to the Klondike. In a movement crowded with rumours of sudden wealth, he attended to the routes, work and makeshift arrangements by which people actually reached the diggings.
en.orientation: His life extended well beyond gold-rush reporting. The study of birchbark canoes and their builders gave his visual precision another, lasting field.
origin: Born in the United States, he developed strong ties to New Brunswick. Art and natural history formed the background to his work as an observer.
career: The Yukon journey placed him inside the gold rush as a reporter. Later work preserved detailed knowledge of canoe construction and indigenous technical traditions.
literature: The Klondike Stampede combines the eyewitness narrative with the illustrator’s power to make a process visible. Equipment and labour keep the story close to the ground.
en.legacy: Adney’s value lies in his resistance to the vague picture. A route, a boat or a method of working becomes something that can be understood in detail.
en.bridge: The book follows the gold rush through the material experience of travel and labour.
en.description: Adney brought drawing, reporting and close description to the Klondike. In a movement crowded with rumours of sudden wealth, he attended to the routes, work and makeshift arrangements by which people actually reached the diggings.
